# Play a game

Play one seat from the first decision to the result. The server's tools are the
same on every producer and are specified in `protocol/tools.md`. The view and
its decisions are specified in `protocol/README.md`. This skill is the loop
around them: `kingdom-analysis` makes the plan, `play-turn` decides the hard
turns, and this skill decides how much thought each decision gets.

## Ground rules

- Know only what your seat may know. Never call a debugging tool (`inspect`
  or anything that says it reads hidden state), and never use another seat's
  token, even one `new_game` handed you.
- Don't sit down against human opponents unless the operator said to. A
  `REFUSED` error is the server enforcing that, so report it and stop.
- Trust the view over your memory. It tracks every card you could know about,
  including your own deck. Your notes only need to hold the plan.

## 1. Start or rejoin

Call `state` first. If you already have a game in progress, carry on with it.
Otherwise call `new_game` with what the operator asked for (kingdom, bots,
seats). Its result is your first full view.

## 2. Make the plan

Run `kingdom-analysis`, quick version (its steps 1–5), on the kingdom in the
first view. The `CARDS` block has the text of every card. Keep the result as a
short game plan, about ten lines:

- the plan and the reason it beats Big Money here;
- the opening for each split;
- the build order, and the point at which you start greening;
- what to watch for: the opponent's possible attacks or plan, and key or
  contested piles.

The plan is the only thing you carry between decisions. If the game is past
its opening when you join, still write the plan, from the current view.

## 3. Answer decisions

Each `step` result shows what changed and your next decision. Spend thought
where it changes the outcome. A game has roughly 30–60 decisions, and most of
them are routine.

- **Routine**: the plan already settles it and nothing in view cares about
  the choice. Examples are playing Treasures when no card reacts to their
  order, ending a phase with nothing worth playing, or the only sensible play.
  Answer it straight away.
- **Turn plan**: at the start of a turn with real choices (Actions to order,
  a buy the plan doesn't settle), work out the whole turn with `play-turn`.
  Then answer its decisions in order. Re-plan only when a draw or a reveal
  changes what you know.
- **Full check**: run `play-turn`'s endgame and attack-response steps when the
  decision is any of these:
  - a buy or gain once the game could end within two turns;
  - a response to an attack;
  - a choice involving a card you haven't judged yet (new `CARDS` lines, an
    unplanned Loot or Reward, a card the opponent just started buying).

Mechanics:

- Read indices from the latest `DECISION` only. They change from one decision
  to the next.
- Check each group's `min` and `max`. `indices: []` chooses nothing. For an
  ordered decision, list the top card first.
- After a `REJECTED` error, read the reason and the decision that came with
  it, then answer that. Don't resend the same answer.
- On `WAITING`, call `wait`. Call `state` only when you've lost track: it
  prints everything. Use `log` for older history.

## 4. Revisit the plan

Check the plan against the view, in one line, at each of these moments:

- the opponent's opening is visible (after their second turn), and whenever
  they start buying something new;
- your deck starts drawing itself, so it is time to switch to payload;
- a pile you or they need runs low;
- someone buys the first Victory card.

When the plan changes, say what changed and why, and update it.

## 5. Finish and review

On `GAME OVER`, report to the operator:

- the result line (VP, turns, how the game ended);
- the plan you made, and whether you kept to it;
- the one or two turns or decisions that decided the game, each with what you
  would do differently, if anything;
- anything the server got wrong or showed confusingly (a missing card text, a
  decision you couldn't express), so the producer can be fixed.

Keep the report short. Don't write lessons into the repository unless asked.

## Talking to the operator during play

Say little while playing. Report the plan once it is made, any change to it,
and the result. If the server breaks (errors that aren't about your answer, a
game that stops advancing), stop and report what you called and what came
back, rather than guessing around it.

# Kingdom analysis

Turn a kingdom into a recommended plan, an opening for each split the
starting deck can produce, and the risks to watch. Rely on the repo context
(`context/rules.md`, `context/strategy.md`, `context/card-power.md` and
`context/combos.md`). This skill adds the procedure. Once the game starts,
use the `play-turn` skill for each decision.

Defaults, unless the user says otherwise:

- Assume 2 players. Name what would change with more players.
- Do the quick analysis (steps 1–5). Go deeper (steps 6–8) when the user
  asks for a full analysis, or when step 5 leaves two plans close or rests
  on a guess about how fast a plan is.
- Work from card text. Community ratings come in at step 4, as a check on a
  view you have already formed.
- Keep the reasoning short and checkable. Don't give a tutorial. A short
  write-up shortens each slot of the output format, never drops one.

## 1. Inventory

- List every Kingdom pile with its cost, plus every landscape (Events,
  Projects, Ways, Landmarks, Traits, Allies, Prophecies) and any non-Supply
  piles they bring (Spoils, Horses, Loot, Rewards, Spirits, ...).
- Note setup effects: Colony/Platinum, Shelters, Heirlooms, Young Witch's
  Bane, a Prophecy and its Sun count, which pile a Trait is on, split piles,
  and added piles (Approaching Army, Ferryman, Riverboat, ...).
- Note special rules in play: Debt, Potion, Night, Favors, Exile, Coffers,
  Villagers, Durations.
- Note the price points: which costs are crowded (every key card at $5) and
  which are empty (nothing worth buying at $2, nothing above $5).
- Write down the actual starting deck and the turn 1–2 splits it produces.
  The default is 4/3 or 5/2, but Heirlooms and Shelters change the deck, and
  some change the money.
- Get exact card text from the user, the log or the client. Never
  reconstruct it from memory. If text is missing, ask or state your
  assumption.

## 2. First read: what is this board about?

Answer these quickly from the card text, before studying any card in depth.
The answers decide where to look harder.

1. **Scoring and ending**: every way to score here (Provinces or Colonies,
   other Victory cards, VP tokens, Landmarks, Curses as minus points), and
   which of them add no card to the deck. Which piles will run out, and how
   does the game most likely end?
2. **Payload**: the biggest sources of $, gains or VP per turn. Is there
   +Buy or gaining to cash in a big turn? One Province per turn is a
   ceiling, not a plan.
3. **Draw and Actions**: which combination of cards actually increases hand
   size without costing Actions (see "Engines" in `context/strategy.md`)?
   Which villages are there, including conditional ones?
4. **Trashing**: is there any, and how fast is it?
5. **Attacks**: is there a junker? Can it be blocked, trashed away or
   outpaced? What do the other attacks hit?
6. **Standouts**: a card the whole board bends around, an unusual setup, a
   landscape that changes scoring, or a way to end the game fast.

Then write one or two sentences: what the board is about, and what is still
open ("the only village is conditional", "no +Buy", "the payoff needs a
discard outlet"). Those open points are what step 3 goes looking for.

## 3. Work backwards from the payload

For each scoring route and payload source from step 2, ask:

- What is the most this could do in one turn if the rest of the board
  served it?
- What stands in the way: Actions, hand size, having it in hand every turn,
  its price, the number of gains?
- Which card or landscape here removes that obstacle?

To answer the third question, read cards for what they **supply** and what
they **want**, not only for their role:

- Supplies: gains (and where they land: discard, hand, top of deck),
  discards from hand or deck, trashes, putting cards on top of the deck or
  ordering it, playing another card, extra Actions or Buys, tokens, anything
  carried to the next turn, forced discards or gains for the opponent.
- Wants: when-gained, when-discarded and when-trashed triggers; counts of
  cards, types or names; a particular cost or type in hand, in play or on
  top of the deck; an Action-dense hand; an Action already in play; a pile
  running out; the opponent doing something.

Consistency is a supply too. Cards that put cards on the deck, order it, set
cards aside or act at the start of the next turn can make one key card show
up every turn, and that is often what makes an awkward engine work.

Write each real interaction as a loop with numbers: "A does X, which
triggers B, for Y per turn, from about turn T".

## 4. Sweep what's left

Step 3 finds what you were looking for. This pass finds what you weren't.

- For every card and landscape that step 3 didn't use, answer in one line:
  which other card here makes this better than its text alone? "None" is an
  allowed answer only after checking it against each of the others. Read the
  whole card first: the type line, the text below the dividing line, and
  where it goes when gained.
- Check the patterns in `context/strategy.md` ("Interactions to look for")
  and the combos in `context/combos.md`. That list shows kinds of
  interaction and is not complete. Don't drop an interaction because it
  isn't listed.
- Look the cards up with `grep -i '<name>' data/card-glicko/*.csv`. Where
  your view and the rating differ by a lot, in either direction, take a
  second look and give the board-specific reason. A rating is never a
  reason to skip a card or to buy one. Ratings marked "deprecated" or with
  a large `phi` carry little weight.

If the sweep turns up a new loop, take it back through step 3.

## 5. Decide

- **Candidates**: two or three plans that are realistic here. Always
  include the strongest Big Money + X as the baseline, and one plan for
  each strong loop. Build the best version of each before judging it: the
  right opening, the cheapest set of pieces, every helper the board offers.
  For each, say how it works, what it needs by when (including the minimum
  number of copies of any scarce card, and whether the opponent wants them
  too), and its main weakness. Write every candidate down, even in a short
  write-up. A recommendation with no rivals beside it skipped this step.
- **No village**: when step 2 found no way to play two terminals in a turn,
  the realistic plans are mostly money decks and the choice of X matters
  most. If the board has an attack, compare at least X as a draw card, X as
  the attack, and two copies of the attack. Give each a rough worked line:
  the opening, the turns it first hits $6 and $8, and how often it plays
  its attack. k copies in an N-card deck reach a 5-card hand in at most
  5k/N of turns, less once copies collide (one copy in 15 cards: 1 turn in
  3; two copies: over half). Judge each against an opponent who also plays
  money (see "The Big Money baseline" in `context/strategy.md`).
- **Pick** the plan with the best result against the opponent's best
  response. Against a strong opponent prefer a plan that holds up whatever
  they do.
- **Openings**: the best opening for each split from step 1, with one line
  of reasoning each. If a split leaves nothing worth buying at one price,
  say so.
- **Buy priorities** for the first two or three shuffles, and roughly when
  to start greening.
- **Ending**: which piles could empty, who benefits, and how the game ends.
- **What would flip the choice**: a different split, the opponent's
  opening, more players, a key pile running low.
- **Least sure of**: the one conclusion most likely to be wrong, and what
  would show it. If that is the choice between two plans, or a guess about
  speed, go on to step 6 for those plans.

## Going deeper

### 6. Play the candidates out

Don't estimate speed from impressions. Play a solo game on paper with
average draws, for every candidate you are comparing and most carefully for
the one that is hardest to estimate (usually the engine). Comparing a worked
money plan with a guessed engine always favors the money plan.

- Turns 1 to about 8, one line per turn: the money or key cards in hand,
  what you play, what you buy or gain, and the deck list after each shuffle.
- One typical built turn, card by card, with the resulting $, Buys and VP.
- If the line stalls (a price never reached, a key card missing its
  shuffle, terminals colliding), try to fix it with what the board offers
  before you call the plan slow.

Read these off the lines you wrote:

- **Speed**: the turn it starts scoring in earnest, and the earliest turn it
  can realistically end the game, or force the opponent to.
- **Scoring rate and ceiling**: VP per turn at its peak, and how much VP is
  actually available to it. A money plan wins by taking about half the
  available VP before the opponent's big turns arrive, so VP that keeps
  scaling (Colonies, VP tokens, Fairgrounds-style alt VP) raises that bar
  and favors engines.
- **Where the curves cross**: money scores early and flattens, engines
  score late and steeply, slogs score slowly for a long time, rushes score
  little and race to the end. The crossing point is when the slower plan
  must be ahead.

### 7. Test the pick against the opponent's best plan

Name the best plan against your pick and judge the matchup. Do the same for
the runner-up. A full grid of every plan against every other is only worth
it with three or more live plans.

- **Race**: does the faster plan end the game, or take an unbeatable lead,
  before the slower one comes online? Use the Big Money clock in
  `context/strategy.md` as the baseline.
- **Interference**: attacks that hit one plan much harder than the other,
  and anything of yours that helps the opponent.
- **Shared resources**: contested piles, mirrored attacks, and three-pile
  risk created by either side.
- **Game-length control**: who decides when the game ends.

Patterns to check: a slog wants the money deck to buy out the Provinces. A
slog or rush threatens a three-pile before an engine is online. In
alternative-VP mirrors the split of the VP pile decides the game. An engine
shouldn't panic-green against money, and should green earlier in a mirror.

### 8. Challenge the result

- Make one more attempt at the rejected plan with the highest ceiling,
  using the fix-ups from step 6. Most wrong calls on a board come from
  rejecting the stronger, harder plan after a shallow look.
- Ask how your pick loses, and whether the opponent can see that from your
  opening.

## Output format

Quick analysis:

```markdown
**Board:** <what it is about, from step 2, in 2–3 sentences>
**Key interactions:**
- <A + B: the loop, with numbers>
**Other cards:** <one line each: its best partner here, or "none">
**Plans considered:** <each in one line: how it works · rough line ($6 and
$8 turns, attack plays) · needs · weakness>
**Recommendation:** <plan, and why it holds up against the best response>
**Open:** <split>: <cards> · <split>: <cards>
**Buy priorities:** <first two or three shuffles, then when to green>
**Ending:** <how it ends, which piles are at risk>
**Watch out for:** <1–3 risks, and what would change the plan>
**Least sure of:** <the conclusion most likely to be wrong, and the test>
**Assumed:** <rules readings or card text you weren't sure of, and anything
you needed that the repo context didn't cover>
```

A deeper analysis adds, before the recommendation:

```markdown
### Build lines
- **<plan>**: T1–2 <buys> · T3–4 <...> · ... · built turn: <$, Buys, VP>

| Plan | Starts scoring | Can end by | Peak VP/turn | VP ceiling |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ... | ~T10 | ~T16 | Province+Duchy | all Provinces + Duchies |

**Against their best plan:** <the matchup for the pick and the runner-up>
**Challenged:** <the rejected plan you re-tested, and how the pick loses>
```

# Play a turn

Turn the current game state into a play sequence and a buy, with a one-line
reason for each decision that isn't obvious. Rely on the repo context,
especially `context/strategy.md` for the plan and the endgame.

## 1. Read the situation

- Get the hand, cards in play, Durations and mats, and whatever is known
  about your deck and discard pile: their size, what's left in the deck
  since the last shuffle, and good cards waiting in the discard.
- Get the scores, the pile counts (Provinces/Colonies and any pile close to
  empty), and your available Actions, Buys, $, Coffers, Villagers and
  Favors.
- Use the card text supplied with the state. Don't reconstruct it from
  memory. If something needed is missing, say what you assumed.
- Decide what this turn is for: building, greening, or ending the game.
  Name the price or gains it needs (e.g. "$8 + a Buy", "gain 2 villages").
- When a card that wasn't part of the plan shows up (a Black Market reveal,
  a Loot, a Reward, a card an attack hands you, something the opponent just
  started buying), check it against the board before judging it: what here
  supplies what it wants, and what wants what it supplies? See
  "Interactions to look for" in `context/strategy.md`. A card that is weak
  on most boards can be the best buy on this one.

## 2. Order the plays

- Play draw first, so later choices are made with the most information.
  Play villages before terminals as needed to keep Actions.
- Play cards that trash from your hand last, so you've seen the most
  targets.
- Hold Throne Room or King's Court until you know what you lack. The best
  target is often another multiplier, or a card that produces what this
  turn still needs.
- Play a gainer just before a reshuffle if you want the gained card soon,
  and late if you don't.
- With more than one Buy, or before buying an Event or Project, play all
  the Treasures you mean to use before the first purchase. Buying anything
  ends Treasure play for the turn (`context/rules.md`, "Buy phase"), so
  paying for one purchase with just the Treasures it needs strands the
  rest. Hold back only a Treasure that hurts you to play.

## 3. Control the reshuffle

- Cards in your hand or in play when you reshuffle miss that whole pass
  through your deck. Trigger a reshuffle when your discard pile is strong
  and your hand is weak, not right after a big turn put your best cards in
  play.
- Don't fill your discard with junk (Cellar, Warehouse) just before you
  draw into a reshuffle.
- Cards that reveal or look at several cards (Sentry) reshuffle as soon as
  fewer cards are left than they look at.
- When buying: if a few cards remain in your deck, your next hand is mostly
  those cards plus the top of the new shuffle. Buy what improves that hand.
  Early in the game, buy what improves your very next shuffle.

## 4. Don't play everything

- Skip plays that hurt you, such as forced trashing of a card you need, or
  that help the opponent, such as a "steal or swap" attack while they hold a
  Province, or effects that give them cards.
- With one Buy, once you've reached your price, consider stopping so good
  cards stay in your deck for next turn.
- Don't play dead cards that only reveal information to the opponent.

## 5. Choose the buy or gains

- Follow the plan from the kingdom analysis, adjusted to what has happened
  since: did the opponent commit to a plan, did a key pile run low?
- When a buy departs from the plan (a card it didn't name, or a default
  such as Silver in place of a card it did), give a one-line reason. If no
  reason holds up, buy what the plan says.
- Before buying a terminal, count the terminals in your deck including
  this one. Without villages, keep to roughly one per 8–10 cards
  (`context/strategy.md`, "Terminal collision"). Past that, a new
  terminal collides often enough that Treasure or a non-terminal is
  usually the better buy.
- Before a scoring buy, check the endgame (`context/strategy.md`, "Greening
  and the endgame"):
  - the Penultimate Province Rule and its exceptions;
  - the opponent's whole next turn: unused extra turns, stored Coffers,
    Villagers or Favors, cards on mats, and the +Buys and Golds left in
    their current shuffle;
  - three-pile risk: how many gains each player needs to end the game.
- Decide whether to spend or keep Coffers and Villagers for a later price
  point or a bigger turn.

## 6. Responding to attacks

- **Discard attacks** (Militia): keep the best three-card *hand*, not the
  three best cards. A deck that draws can keep Village + Smithy and discard
  Golds.
- **Junking**: when given a choice (e.g. Torturer), don't always take the
  option that keeps your deck clean if it costs you your own key plays.
- Reveal Reactions only when the benefit beats keeping the card's normal
  use.

## Output format

```markdown
**Goal this turn:** <e.g. "$8 + Buy for Province + Duchy">
**Play:** 1. <card> — <why, if not obvious> 2. ...
**Buy/gain:** <cards> — <why; for a terminal, the count against deck size;
for a departure from the plan, the reason>
**Watch:** <endgame or reshuffle notes, if any>
```

If the best line depends on unknown information, give the line for the
likely case and say what would change it.

I won, 44 VP to 37. We each took 19 turns, and the game ended when I bought the last Province.

**Kingdom:** Messenger, Sack of Loot, Chariot Race, Clerk, Ghost Town, Artificer, Catacombs, Village, Hoard, Black Cat, plus Road Network (Project) and Way of the Horse (Way). Nothing on the board trashes cards, and the only village was plain Village, so I didn't build an engine.

**Plan:** Big Money with two Clerks, Sack of Loot and Gold, opening Silver/Clerk. I kept to it, except that I never bought the Black Cats I'd planned. A Cat would have been in my hand on only about one bot turn in six, so a flat Estate was worth more. Clerk paid off: it can be played free at the start of my turn, so two copies never collided.

**What decided it:** The bot drew $8–9 early and led 24 to 15 by turn 11. Two choices brought me back:
- **Turns 12 and 14:** I spent $10 on two Duchies rather than a Province plus a Black Cat. That kept 3 Provinces in the pile, and the longer game favoured my stronger deck (four Golds and Loot against its two Golds).
- **Turn 18:** I used Way of the Horse on a Clerk to reach $7, bought a Gold and put it on top of my deck with Insignia. The bot then took the second-last Province to tie at 37. That Gold helped me reach $13 the next turn for the last Province and an Estate.

**Problems with the tools:**
1. **Unlabelled options:** every Clerk start-of-turn decision had a mandatory `[reject-ability] Resolve an effect (choose 1)  5: 0  6: 1` group with no labels, plus a second `[way]` group. It wasn't clear what answering it would do.
2. **Buy list leaves out some treasures:** on turn 9 the header said "$7 available", but the buy list stopped at $4 because Puzzle Box wasn't counted.
3. **Cost shown as value:** the play list shows each treasure's cost, not what it makes ("Silver $3", "Puzzle Box $7"), which reads like the money it produces.
4. **Autoplay skipped Shield:** after "Autoplay Treasures" the log showed "plays a Copper and a Gold (+$4)" and left Shield, a plain +$3 +Buy treasure, in my hand.
5. **No Loot text:** `CARDS` gave "Loot Pile: no card text on record", so I couldn't value Sack of Loot until each Loot turned up.
